meeting_header: Date: 2028-02-14 | Start: 16:30 PST | Duration: 59m | Location: Zoom | Attendees: Alex Rivera (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Tomislav Novak (Redwood SE), Chris Patel (Zenolith CTO), Jordan Ellis (Zenolith Platform Lead), Sasha Nguyen (Zenolith Security)
summary: Discovery focused on integration patterns for Zenolith's customer-facing inference gateway. Main topics: SDK fit (node/python), LangChain/LlamaIndex connector compatibility, gateway/proxy architecture, burst rate limits and quota behavior, observability hooks and token-level cost telemetry, and private vs hosted tradeoffs. Zenolith wants a low-friction pilot with predictable latency under bursty traffic and clear security posture for SOC2 + KMS. Action: Redwood to run benchmarks, share security docs, and schedule VPC deep dive.
topics: Integration approach (SDKs + middleware), LangChain & LlamaIndex adapters, gateway/proxy routing, rate limits/quota design, observability & traces, private deployment and KMS, canary rollout strategy
transcript_body:
[00:00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick round robin who we have.
[00:00:08] Chris - Zenolith (CTO): Chris here, hi. We're excited to understand how Redwood would slot into our gateway.
[00:00:12] Jordan - Zenolith: Jordan, platform. We're the team owning the API gateway and LLM orchestration.
[00:00:18] Sasha - Zenolith (Security): Sasha from security — we'll focus on encryption, audit logs, and compliance.
[00:00:25] Maya (Redwood SE): Hi all, Maya — I'll be running the tech deep dives and benchmarks.
[00:00:29] Tomislav (Redwood SE): Tomislav — I'll jump in on batching and runtime details.
[00:00:35] Alex: Great. Agenda: quick product fit, then dive into integration patterns — SDK vs gateway, LangChain/LlamaIndex connectors, rate limits, and observability.
[00:00:48] Chris: High level: Zenolith has a customer-facing gateway that fans out to multiple models. We want to route to hosted Redwood for most tenants, but reserve a private VPC path for regulated customers. Need fast failover and predictable cost.
[00:01:05] Jordan: We currently proxy through our envoy layer and attach custom auth. We prefer a proxy-first approach to avoid touching app code for many services.
[00:01:16] Alex: Totally makes sense. Two main integration patterns we've seen: 1) Direct SDK / server-side libs (node/python) embedded in service, 2) Gateway/proxy adapter that translates internal requests to Redwood API. Both are compatible with LangChain/LlamaIndex downstream usage.
[00:01:33] Jordan: For us, minimal changes to app code is preferred — gateway adapter sounds best. How does Redwood handle auth from a proxy?
[00:01:41] Maya: You can use a single service token on the gateway and map per-tenant principals with headers if you need rate limits and per-tenant quotas. For private deployments you'd use short-lived creds and integrate with your KMS / HSM for signing.
[00:01:55] Sasha: On KMS: our policy requires customer keys for PII handling. For private option, does Redwood support customer-managed KMS/HSM?
[00:02:03] Alex: Yes, Private deployments support customer-managed KMS. For Hosted we encrypt at rest with our keys but can integrate with BYOK for Dedicated/Private in the roadmap and current private package.
[00:02:14] [00:02:20] Tomislav: Quick note on pf caching — we do prefix/KV cache to reduce repeated token cost. That matters if you're doing retrieval augmented generation. We've seen 40-60% cost reduction in some workloads.
[00:02:36] Jordan: Nice. Regarding LangChain and LlamaIndex, our retrieval pipelines use LlamaIndex. Are there connector examples?
[00:02:44] Maya: We have SDK adapters and community examples for both. For LlamaIndex you can swap the llm wrapper to call Redwood's python SDK or straight HTTP. A few customers use a small shim in the gateway that supports both.
[00:02:58] Chris: If we go shim-in-gateway, how do you handle streaming and partial responses? Important for our UX.
[00:03:05] Tomislav: Streaming is supported in both SDKs and the HTTP API. On the gateway, you can stream through (chunked response) or buffer for per-tenant rate shaping. Note: very long lived streaming sessions interact with KV cache eviction so we tune keepalive.
[00:03:22] [00:03:28] Jordan: Talk to me about quotas and rate limits. We have bursty patterns — up to 1.2k rps sustained for a few 10s minutes, and occasional spikes to 3k rps. We need predictable throttling.
[00:03:40] Maya: We support rate limiting at multiple layers: service-level quotas, token-based billing thresholds, and per-API-key enforcement. For Hosted, our quota subsystem can enforce spikes with backpressure and automatic fallback to a lower-cost model variant. For Dedicated, you get reserved GPU pools and more predictable throughput.
[00:03:59] Chris: Automatic fallback — can it fallback to a cheaper quantized model without changing the API contract?
[00:04:06] Tomislav: Yes: we surface model variants that are API-compatible. On overload the routing policy can route to the variant and we tag responses so you can track quality regressions.
[00:04:17] Sasha: On audit logs — we need immutable request/response logs for a sample of traffic, plus redaction. How are PII redaction and logging controls exposed?
[00:04:26] Alex: You can configure redact rules in the private console or via the API. For Hosted, sample-level logging and redaction policies are available; for Private you control full logs locally. We also provide exportable audit logs for compliance.
[00:04:40] Chris: Can Redwood plug into our existing tracing setup? We use Jaeger + OpenTelemetry.
[00:04:45] Maya: Yes — Redwood has observability hooks: request IDs, token-level cost breakdowns, latency histograms per model, and OpenTelemetry spans you can push into your collector. For Dedicated/Private we can forward traces directly.
[00:04:58] Jordan: About SDKs — do we lose batching benefits if we go through a gateway shim?
[00:05:04] Tomislav: Good question. Batching is best handled at the runtime side; our gateway shim can emit batched requests if it's aware of request patterns. Continuous batching benefits more when requests are pooled at the server side, but gateway can implement client-side batching strategies that still get KV cache hits. There's a tradeoff with added latency for batching windows.
[00:05:22] [00:05:27] Chris: We want end-to-end SLO: 95th percentile < 220ms for short completions. Can Redwood meet that on Hosted under our expected load?
[00:05:35] Maya: We'll need to run a benchmark with your exact prompt and length distribution. We have a performance profile for our curated models — short prompts can be served under 200ms p95 in many regions, but it depends on model size, quantization, batching, and network path.
[00:05:49] Alex: For Dedicated you can guarantee lower variance with reserved capacity. Hosted is cost efficient but bursts may see routing variance. We'll propose both options in the follow up.
[00:05:58] Jordan: On billing — we want token-level breakdowns for cost attribution to customers. Is that accessible?
[00:06:03] Maya: Yes, Console shows token-level cost and latency per request. We can also stream that telemetry to a billing data pipeline.
[00:06:10] Sasha: Legal will ask about data residency. Can Hosted restrict region to EU only?
[00:06:15] Alex: Hosted can pin to region in many of our cloud regions; for strict data residency and air-gapped needs, Private is the option.
[00:06:22] [00:06:27] Jordan: Let's talk about a pilot. We want to run a 2-week pilot for non-PHI customers via Hosted behind our gateway adapter, then evaluate Dedicated for regulated tenants. Steps?
[00:06:36] Alex: Typical flow: Redwood provisions a sandbox org, we give you a service token and SDK examples for a gateway shim, Maya runs the baseline perf, then we instrument observability hooks. During pilot we can evaluate failover to dedicated reserved pools if needed.
[00:06:48] Chris: For pilot success criteria: p95 latency <= 250ms, no more than 2% errors under 1.5k sustained QPS, and token cost within our budget target.
[00:06:58] Maya: We'll run targeted load tests and provide a report with latency and cost breakdowns.
[00:07:04] Tomislav: Also recommend instrumenting a small set of golden prompts for quality monitoring — Redwood Optimize can alert on regressions if generation distributions change.
[00:07:13] Sasha: Security follow ups: we need the network diagram, SAML/SSO options, and whether you support SCIM for provisioning.
[00:07:20] Alex: We'll send SAML + SCIM docs and a network topology. We also have a private deployment checklist for KMS and ingress egress rules.
[00:07:27] Jordan: A couple of nitty gritty items — do you support per-tenant rate shaping (token or request based)? And can we configure quota windows (minute/hour/day)?
[00:07:35] Maya: Yes; per-tenant quotas can be request-based or token-based. Quota windows are configurable and you can set hard vs soft limits with webhook callbacks for soft-limit warnings.
[00:07:45] Chris: On the gateway side, we want the shim to include a small local cache of KV vectors to avoid repeating retrieval calls. Any guidance?
[00:07:52] Tomislav: For retrieval-augmented flows, keeping a local vector cache for top-k hits is common. Redwood's KV / prefix cache is complementary — you can use both. Watch for staleness and cache invalidation.
[00:08:02] [00:08:10] Chris: Are there any gotchas with LlamaIndex? We've seen tokenization mismatches in a few setups.
[00:08:16] Maya: Tokenization differences usually come from model family mismatches. Use the same tokenizer in LlamaIndex layer and the model. Our SDK exposes tokenizer metadata and we include examples to normalize.
[00:08:27] Jordan: Can we run an A/B where 10% of traffic routes to Redwood Hosted and 90% stays internal?
[00:08:33] Alex: Yes — rollout policies support canary and percentage-based routing; we also provide automatic fallback policies if quality or latency crosses thresholds.
[00:08:41] Sasha: About redaction in logs again — can we send logs to our SIEM while redacting PII at Redwood side?
[00:08:48] Maya: Yes — we support log forwarding with transformation rules and we can apply server-side redaction prior to export. For Private you'd control that entirely.
[00:08:58] [00:09:05] Jordan: One last thing — cost control: do you have automatic batching/caching recommendations or a cost simulator?
[00:09:12] Tomislav: Redwood Optimize gives suggestions — recommended batching windows, quantization for models, and caching strategies. We also provide a cost simulator based on prompt distributions.
[00:09:22] Chris: Great. Let's talk timelines. If we start pilot next week, get results by end of month?
[00:09:28] Alex: Feasible — we'll provision sandbox today if you confirm. Maya: I'll start the benchmark as soon as we get the sample prompts and traffic profile.
[00:09:36] Sasha: I'll review the security docs once received.
[00:09:40] Alex: Cool. Recap and next steps?
[00:09:42] [00:09:45] Maya: Action: benchmark with Zenolith prompts (Maya), share perf report.
[00:09:50] Alex: I'll send SOC2, SAML/SCIM docs, and the private deployment checklist. Also include SDK/gateway shim examples for Node+Python.
[00:09:58] Jordan: We'll provide prompt sets, size distributions, and expected QPS.
[00:10:03] Chris: Schedule VPC deep dive next week.
[00:10:06] Alex: Sounds good — thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with links to sandbox and docs.
[00:10:12] Speaker 4: (background) thanks
[00:10:15] [END OF TRANSCRIPT - call lasted ~59 minutes, transcript truncated here for brevity]
